{{Short description|Model of the elements of the solar system}}
A '''fundamental ephemeris''' of the [[Solar System]] is a [[Computer simulation|model]] of the objects of the system in space, with all of their positions and motions accurately represented. It is intended to be a high-precision primary reference for prediction and observation of those positions and motions, and which provides a basis for further refinement of the model. It is generally not intended to cover the entire life of the Solar System; usually a short-duration time span, perhaps a few centuries, is represented to high accuracy. Some long ephemerides cover several millennia to medium accuracy.

They are published by the [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] as [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory Development Ephemeris|Development Ephemeris]]. The latest releases include DE430 which covers planetary and lunar ephemeris from Dec 21, 1549 to Jan 25, 2650 with high precision and is intended for general use for modern time periods . DE431 was created to cover a longer time period Aug 15, -13200 to March 15, 17191 with slightly less precision for use with historic observations and far reaching forecasted positions.  DE432 was released as a minor update to DE430 with improvements to the Pluto barycenter in support of the [[New Horizons]] mission.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/generic_kernels/spk/planets/de432.pdf|title=JPL Memo IOM 392R-14-003|last=Folkner|date=April 30, 2014}}</ref>

==Description==
The set of physical laws and numerical constants used in the calculation of the ephemeris must be self-consistent and precisely specified. The ephemeris must be calculated strictly in accordance with this set, which represents the most current knowledge of all relevant physical forces and effects. Current fundamental ephemerides are typically released with exact descriptions of all mathematical models, methods of computation, observational data, and adjustment to the observations at the time of their announcement.<ref>See, for instance, {{cite web|url=http://iau-comm4.jpl.nasa.gov/de405iom/de405iom.pdf |title=JPL Planetary and Lunar Ephemerides DE405/LE405 |author=Standish |date=1998 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120220062549/http://iau-comm4.jpl.nasa.gov/de405iom/de405iom.pdf |archivedate=2012-02-20 }}; {{cite web|url=http://www.imcce.fr/inpop/inpop10a.pdf |title=INPOP10a |author=Fienga |display-authors=etal |date=2010 }}; {{cite web|url=http://iau-comm4.jpl.nasa.gov/EPM2004.pdf |title=High-Precision Ephemerides of Planets—EPM and Determination of Some Astronomical Constants |author=Pitjeva |date=2004 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20081031065523/http://iau-comm4.jpl.nasa.gov/EPM2004.pdf |archivedate=2008-10-31 }}</ref> This may not have been the case in the past, as fundamental ephemerides were then computed from a collection of methods derived over a span of decades by many researchers.<ref name="sandw">{{cite web |url=ftp://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/eph/planets/ioms/ExplSupplChap8.pdf |author=Standish and Williams |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200810042008/ftp://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/eph/planets/ioms/ExplSupplChap8.pdf |archive-date=2020-08-10 |url-status=dead |title=CHAPTER 8: Orbital Ephemerides of the Sun, Moon, and Planets |date=2010}} A chapter from an as-yet-unpublished (Feb 2012) version of the ''Explanatory Supplement'' (see [[#Sources|Sources]])</ref>

The independent variable of the ephemeris is always time. In the case of the most current ephemerides, it is a [[Coordinate time|relativistic coordinate time]] scale equivalent to the [[International Astronomical Union|IAU]] definition of [[Barycentric Coordinate Time|TCB]].<ref name="sandw" /> In the past, [[Solar time|mean solar time]] (before the discovery of the non-uniform [[rotation of the Earth]]) and [[ephemeris time]] (before the implementation of [[Post-Newtonian expansion|relativistic gravitational equations]]) were used. The remainder of the ephemeris can consist of either the mathematical equations and initial conditions which describe the motions of the bodies of the Solar System, of tabulated data calculated from those equations and conditions, or of condensed mathematical representations of the tabulated data.

A fundamental ephemeris is the basis from which apparent ephemerides, phenomena, and orbital elements are computed for astronomical, nautical, and surveyors' almanacs. Apparent ephemerides give positions and motions of Solar System bodies as seen by observers from the surface of Earth, and are useful for astronomers, navigators, and surveyors in planning observations and in reducing the data acquired, although much of the work of latter two has been supplanted by [[Global Positioning System|GPS]] technology. Phenomena are events related to the configurations of Solar System bodies, for instance [[Sunrise|rise]] and [[Sunset|set]] times, [[Lunar phase|phases]], [[eclipse]]s and [[occultation]]s, and have many civil and scientific applications. [[Orbital elements]] are descriptions of the motion of a body at a particular instant, used for further short-time-span calculation of the body's position when high accuracy is not required.

==History==
Astronomers have been tasked with computing accurate ephemerides, originally for purposes of sea navigation, from at least the 18th century. In England, [[Charles II of England|Charles II]] founded the [[Royal Observatory, Greenwich|Royal Observatory]] in 1675,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rmg.co.uk/royal-observatory/history/ |title=History of the Royal Observatory, Greenwich|date=14 September 2015}}</ref> which began publishing ''[[The Nautical Almanac]]'' in 1766.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://aa.usno.navy.mil/publications/docs/na_history.php |title=History of The Nautical Almanac |access-date=2012-02-10 |archivedate=2009-06-18 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090618142559/http://aa.usno.navy.mil/publications/docs/na_history.php |url-status=deviated }}</ref> In France, the ''[[Bureau des Longitudes]]'' was founded in 1795 to publish the ''[[Connaissance des Temps]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.imcce.fr/en/presentation/histoire_imcce.php |title=History of the IMCCE |access-date=2012-02-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120227075923/http://www.imcce.fr/en/presentation/histoire_imcce.php |archive-date=2012-02-27 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The early fundamental ephemerides of these publications came from many different sources and authors as the science of [[celestial mechanics]] matured.<ref>See ''Explanatory Supplement'' (1961), chap. 7 or ''Explanatory Supplement'' (1992), chap. 13 for extensive lists of sources of the early fundamental ephemerides of the ''Nautical Almanac''. (see [[#Sources|Sources]])</ref>

At the end of the 19th century, the analytical methods of [[Perturbation (astronomy)|general perturbations]] reached the probable limits of what could be accomplished by hand calculation. The planetary "theories" of [[Simon Newcomb|Newcomb]]<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zKoUAQAAMAAJ |last=Newcomb |date=1898 |title=Tables of the Motion of the Earth on its Axis and Around the Sun |journal=Astronomical Papers Prepared for the Use of the American Ephemeris and Nautical Almanac |volume=VI |issue=Part I |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office, Washington, DC}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zKoUAQAAMAAJ |last=Newcomb |date=1898 |title=Tables of the Heliocentric Motion of Mercury |journal=Astronom. Papers American Ephem. |volume=VI, part II|issue=2 |pages=171 |bibcode=1898USNAO...6..171N }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zKoUAQAAMAAJ |last=Newcomb |date=1898 |title=Tables of the Heliocentric Motion of Venus |journal=Astronom. Papers American Ephem. |volume=VI, part III|pages=271 |bibcode=1898USNAO...6..271N }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zKoUAQAAMAAJ |last=Newcomb |date=1898 |title=Tables of the Heliocentric Motion of Mars |journal=Astronom. Papers American Ephem. |volume=VI, part IV|issue=4 |pages=383 |bibcode=1898USNAO...6..383N }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tHfmAAAAMAAJ&pg=PP5 |last=Newcomb |date=1898 |title=Tables of the Heliocentric Motion of Uranus |journal=Astronom. Papers American Ephem. |volume=VII|pages=1 |bibcode=1898USNAO...7R...1N }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tHfmAAAAMAAJ&pg=PP5|last=Newcomb |date=1898 |title=Tables of the Heliocentric Motion of Neptune |journal=Astronom. Papers American Ephem. |volume=VII|pages=1 |bibcode=1898USNAO...7Q...1N }}</ref> and [[George William Hill|Hill]]<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tHfmAAAAMAAJ&pg=PP5|last=Hill |date=1898 |title=Tables of Jupiter |journal=Astronom. Papers American Ephem. |volume=VII}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tHfmAAAAMAAJ&pg=PP5|last=Hill |date=1898 |title=Tables of Saturn |journal=Astronom. Papers American Ephem. |volume=VII}}</ref> formed the fundamental ephemerides of the ''Nautical Almanac'' at that time. For the Sun, Mercury, Venus, and Mars, the tabulations of the ''[[Astronomical Almanac]]'' continued to be derived from the work of Newcomb and Ross<ref>{{citation |last=Ross |date=1917 |title=New Elements of Mars |series=Astronom. Papers American Ephem. |volume=IX |issue=Part II}}</ref> through 1983. In France, the works of [[Leverrier|LeVerrier]]<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/iarticle_query?journal=AnPar&volume=0004&type=SCREEN_THMB |title=Théorie et Tables du Mouvement Apparent du Soleil |journal=Annales de l'Observatoire Impérial de Paris |volume=IV |language=French |author=LeVerrier |date=1858}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/iarticle_query?journal=AnPar&volume=0005&type=SCREEN_THMB |title=Théorie et Tables du Mouvement de Mercure |journal=Annales de l'Observatoire Impérial de Paris |volume=V |language=French |author=LeVerrier |date=1859}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/iarticle_query?journal=AnPar&volume=0006&type=SCREEN_THMB |title=Théorie et Tables du Mouvement de Vénus |journal=Annales de l'Observatoire Impérial de Paris, Mémoires |volume=VI |language=French |author=LeVerrier |date=1861}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/iarticle_query?journal=AnPar&volume=0006&type=SCREEN_THMB |title=Théorie et Tables du Mouvement de Mars |journal=Annales de l'Observatoire Impérial de Paris, Mémoires |volume=VI |language=French |author=LeVerrier |date=1861}}</ref><ref>LeVerrier developed and published his original theories of the outer planets in ''Annales de l'Observatoire de Paris, Mémoires |volume=X-|volume=XIV ''</ref> and [[Jean Baptiste Aimable Gaillot|Gaillot]]<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/iarticle_query?journal=AnPar&volume=0031&type=SCREEN_THMB |title=Tables Rectifiées du Mouvement de Jupiter |journal=Annales de l'Observatoire de Paris, Mémoires |volume=XXXI |language=French |author=Gaillot |date=1913}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/iarticle_query?journal=AnPar&volume=0024&type=SCREEN_THMB |title=Tables Rectifiées du Mouvement de Saturne |journal=Annales de l'Observatoire de Paris, Mémoires |volume=XXIV |language=French |author=Gaillot |date=1904}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/iarticle_query?journal=AnPar&volume=0028&type=SCREEN_THMB |title=Tables Nouvelles des Mouvements d'Uranus et de Neptune |journal=Annales de l'Observatoire de Paris, Mémoires |volume=XXVIII|language=French |author=Gaillot |date=1910}}</ref> formed the fundamental ephemeris of the ''Connaissance des Temps''.

From the mid 20th century, work began on [[numerical integration]] of the [[equations of motion]] on [[IBM SSEC|early computing machines]] for purposes of producing fundamental ephemerides for the ''Astronomical Almanac''. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto were based on the work of Eckert, ''et al''.<ref>{{citation |author=Eckert |author2=Brouwer |author3=Clemence |date=1951 |title=Coordinates of the Five Outer Planets 1953–2060 |series=Astronom. Papers American Ephem. |volume=XII}}</ref> and Clemence<ref>{{citation |author=Clemence |date=1954 |title=Perturbations of the Five Outer Planets by the Four Inner Ones |series=Astronom. Papers American Ephem. |volume=XIII |issue=Part V}}</ref> through 1983. The fundamental ephemeris of the Moon, always a difficult problem in celestial mechanics, remained a work-in-progress through the early 1980s. It was based originally on the work of Brown,<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nBFLAAAAYAAJ |author=Brown |date=1919 |title=Tables of the Motion of the Moon |publisher=Yale University Press, New Haven, CT}}</ref> with updates and corrections by Clemence, ''et al''.<ref>{{cite journal |date=1952 |title=Aberration in the Lunar Ephemeris |journal=Astronomical Journal |volume=57 |pages=46–47|bibcode=1952AJ.....57...46C |doi=10.1086/106703 |last1=Clemence |first1=G. M |last2=Porter |first2=J. G |last3=Sadler |first3=D. H |doi-access=free }}</ref> and Eckert, ''et al''.<ref>{{cite journal |bibcode=1966AJ.....71..314E |date=1966 |title=Transformation of the Lunar Coordinates and Orbital Parameters |journal=Astronomical Journal |volume=71 |pages=314–332|doi=10.1086/109923 |last1=Eckert |first1=W. J |last2=Walker |first2=M. J |last3=Eckert |first3=D |doi-access= }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |date=1969 |title=A Note on the Evaluation of the Latitude of the Moon |journal=[[Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society]] |volume=146 |issue=4 |pages=473–478|bibcode=1969MNRAS.146..473E |doi=10.1093/mnras/146.4.473 |last1=Eckert |first1=W. J |last2=Van Flandern |first2=T. C |last3=Wilkins |first3=G. A |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>See also {{citation |author=Nautical Almanac Office, U.S. Naval Observatory |author2=H.M. Nautical Almanac Office, Royal Greenwich Observatory |date=1954 |title=Improved Lunar Ephemeris |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office, Washington, DC}}.</ref>

Starting in 1984, a revolution in the methods of producing fundamental ephemerides began.<ref>See {{cite journal |date=1983 |bibcode=1983A&A...125..150N |title=DE 102 – A numerically integrated ephemeris of the moon and planets spanning forty-four centuries |journal=Astronomy and Astrophysics |volume=125 |issue=1|pages=150 |last1=Newhall |first1=X. X |last2=Standish |first2=E. M |last3=Williams |first3=J. G }} for a good description of the new methods from their early days.</ref> From 1984 through 2002, the fundamental ephemeris of the ''Astronomical Almanac'' was the [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]]'s [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory Development Ephemeris|DE200/LE200]], a fully numerically-integrated ephemeris fitted to modern position and velocity observations of the Sun, Moon, and planets. From 2003 onward (as of Feb 2012), [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory Development Ephemeris|JPL's DE405/LE405]], an integrated ephemeris referred to the [[International Celestial Reference Frame]], has been used.<ref name="sandw" /> In France, the ''Bureau des Longitudes'' began using their machine-generated semi-analytical theory VSOP82 in 1984,<ref>{{cite journal |bibcode=1982A&A...114..278B |title=Théorie du mouvement de l'ensemble des planètes. Solution VSOP82 |journal=Astronomy and Astrophysics |volume=114 |pages=278 |date=1982 |language=French|last1=Bretagnon |first1=P }}</ref> and their work continued with the founding of the ''[[IMCCE|Institut de mécanique céleste et de calcul des éphémérides]]'' in 1998 and the INPOP<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.imcce.fr/inpop/inpop06_preprint.pdf |title=INPOP06. A new numerical planetary ephemeris |author=Fienga |display-authors=etal |date=2006}};  {{cite web |url=http://www.imcce.fr/inpop/inpop08_preprint.pdf |title=INPOP08, a 4-D planetary ephemeris |author=Fienga |display-authors=etal |date=2008}}; {{cite web |url=http://www.imcce.fr/inpop/inpop10a.pdf |title=INPOP10a |author=Fienga |display-authors=etal |date=2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=INPOP17a planetary ephemerides |date=2017 |publisher=Institut de mécanique céleste et de calcul des éphémérides |isbn=978-2-910015-79-4 |url=https://www.imcce.fr/content/medias/recherche/equipes/asd/inpop/inpop17a_v3_090817.pdf}}</ref> series of numerical ephemerides. DE405/LE405 were superseded by DE421/LE421 in 2008.<ref>{{Cite web|url=ftp://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/eph/planets/README.txt|title=JPL Planetary and Lunar Ephemerides|last=Folkner|first=William|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200528163216/ftp://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/eph/planets/README.txt|archive-date=2020-05-28|url-status=dead|date=April 30, 2014}}</ref>
